title: Checkpoint: Going Further
intro: Check that you understand iterators, generators, and regular expressions, and how to structure a text-processing program.

questions.question: What do the two print calls show?
questions.code:
evens = (n for n in range(10) if n % 2 == 0)
print(sum(evens))
print(sum(evens))
questions.explanation: The first sum() exhausts the generator, so the second one sees no values and returns 0.

questions.question: What lines are printed, in order?
questions.code:
def countdown(n):
    print("start")
    while n > 0:
        yield n
        n -= 1

gen = countdown(3)
print("created")
print(next(gen), next(gen))
questions.explanation: Calling a generator function only creates the generator. The body starts running at the first next().

questions.question: What happens when this code runs?
questions.explanation: A list is iterable but not an iterator. Use next(iter(cities)).

questions.question: What does this code print?
questions.code:
def chunks():
    yield from [1, 2]
    yield 3

print(list(chunks()), sum(chunks()))
questions.explanation: yield from produces each item of the list one by one. Each call to chunks() makes a fresh generator, so sum() sees all values.

questions.question: What does this code print?
questions.code:
import re
text = "Total: 45000 som"
print(re.match(r"\d+", text))
questions.explanation: re.match only checks the start of the string, which is not a digit. Use re.search to look anywhere.

questions.question: What does this code print?
questions.code: import re html = "Plov and Somsa" print(re.findall(r"(.*)", html))
questions.explanation: Greedy .* grabs as much as possible, up to the last . Use .*? or [^<]* to stop at the first one.

questions.question: What does this code print?
questions.explanation: match succeeds because the string starts with digits, but fullmatch requires the whole string to match. Use fullmatch for validation.

questions.question: What does this code print?
questions.explanation: Named groups are read by name, and group(0) is the whole match.

questions.question: What does this code print?
questions.code:
from collections import Counter
text = "Plov, plov and more plov!"
print(Counter(text.lower().split())["plov"])
questions.explanation: split() leaves punctuation attached, so "plov," and "plov!" count as different words. Extract words with a regex like [a-z]+.

questions.question: In the text analyzer, where should functions like count_sentences(text) get their data, and where should printing happen?
options: Take text as an argument and return values
Read the file and print inside each function
Store text and results in global variables
Put everything in one main() function
questions.explanation: Pure functions that take arguments and return values are easy to test and reuse. Keep file reading and printing at the edges.
